extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in art and architectural criticism (artists, architects, art-historians, clergy, and educated general readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for judging the form, ornament, color, and religious suitability of church architecture and decoration, with emphasis on Byzantine mosaics and the relationship between domestic and ecclesiastical styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustratability of architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is so rare in art, as ... a fair illustration of architecture; 'perfect' illustration of it does not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architectural effect depends on chiselling adapted to a certain viewing distance; the peculiar interplay of confusion and order produced by distance cannot be faithfully reproduced in plates or small-scale illustrations. Therefore criticism by illustration is intrinsically limited and likely misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and level of detail required for faithful representation
rubrics_metrics.description: In the illustration of details, every building of any pretensions to high architectural rank would require a volume of plates, and those finished with extraordinary care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fragments or small engravings (even enlarged) fail to show sharp folds, minor relief, and fine polychromy; faithful representation demands very large, carefully finished plates or life‑scale casts to convey the true effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color as an essential architectural component (St. Mark's example)
rubrics_metrics.description: St. Mark's effect depends not only upon the most delicate sculpture but eminently on its color ... the most subtle, variable, inexpressible color in the world,--the color of glass, of transparent alabaster, of polished marble, and lustrous gold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color is inseparable from architectural effect in some buildings; reproductions that ignore or cannot convey subtle collation (e.g., quarter-inch glass tesserae mixing blue and green) will fail to communicate the building's true merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of richness of ornament in churches
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether richness of ornament be right in churches at all is a primary question; churches are the only places in which offering a portion of all precious things to God could be legitimately expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rich ornament is defensible because churches legitimately display precious materials, but its effect on worship depends on the congregation's familiarity with beauty; sudden unfamiliar splendor may distract rather than aid devotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: No inherent sacredness in particular architectural forms
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no sacredness in round arches, nor in pointed; none in pinnacles, nor in buttresses; none in pillars, nor in traceries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architectural features are not intrinsically ecclesiastical; they were commonly used in domestic architecture of their periods. Judgments about 'sacred' styles should be based on historical function and adaptation, not mystical associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: A noble style must be applicable to both dwelling and church
rubrics_metrics.description: It must be practised in the dwelling before it be perfected in the church, and it is the test of a noble style that it shall be applicable to both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a style is essentially false it may be tolerated in houses for convenience but will fail when tried in a church; genuine architectural forms should bear daily use and sacred function alike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Byzantine decoration's essential pictorial character
rubrics_metrics.description: Byzantine work leaves large surfaces void of bold architectural features, to be rendered interesting merely by surface ornament or sculpture ... the Byzantine church requires expression and interesting decoration over vast plane surfaces,—decoration which becomes noble only by becoming pictorial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Byzantine architecture depends on pictorial decoration (mosaics, figures, florals) to enliven planes, its fitness for church use depends on the religious effects of pictorial art and the audience's reception of pictorial representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of religious art lies between idolatry and supreme craftsmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective religious art ... has always lain, and I believe must always lie, between the two extremes--of barbarous idol-fashioning on one side, and magnificent craftsmanship on the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful sacred art should avoid crude idolatries (which encourage worship of the object) and also avoid works that draw attention away from the subject into admiration of art itself; suitable forms include missal painting, glass-painting, rude sculpture, mosaics, frescoes and tempera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mosaics and inlay are particularly effective for public religious teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: The great mosaics of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries covered the walls and roofs of the churches with inevitable lustre; they could not be ignored ... their size rendered them majestic, their distance mysterious, their color attractive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-scale mosaics functioned as a 'poor man's Bible'—legible at distance, unavoidable in worship, and therefore highly effective as religious instruction for illiterate congregations; modern use should consider similar didactic visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility rules: bright coloring over chiaroscuro for distant/dim locations
rubrics_metrics.description: The bright coloring and disregard of chiaroscuro cannot be regarded as imperfections, since they are the only means by which the figures could be rendered clearly intelligible in the distance and darkness of the vaulting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In high, dimly lit church interiors, strong flat color increases legibility of figures and narratives; sculptural modelling and refined chiaroscuro that read at close range may fail from the nave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity with beauty in daily life conditions the usefulness of ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: If once familiarized with beautiful form and color ... we shall desire to see this evidence also in whatever is built or labored for the house of prayer; the absence of the accustomed loveliness would disturb instead of assisting devotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce and cultivate beauty in ordinary dwelling and public life so that church ornament becomes a natural continuation rather than a startling novelty which could distract worshippers unaccustomed to such stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of overvaluing polish and academic training over native imaginative power
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to calculate the enormous loss of power in modern days, owing to the imperative requirement that art shall be methodical and learned ... people mistake the polish for the power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow scope for unpolished, imaginative local craftsmen whose crude work may carry genuine religious feeling; excessive emphasis on academy technique can suppress spontaneous, devotional expression valuable in sacred contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural inscriptions should be legible and read
rubrics_metrics.description: Our eyes are now familiar and wearied with writing; and if an inscription is put upon a building, unless it be large and clear, it is ten to one whether we ever trouble ourselves to decipher it. But the old architect was sure of readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inscribed texts on churches were intended to be read and to communicate doctrine or narrative; designers should ensure inscriptions are sufficiently large and clear for intended audiences if they are part of the building's teaching.
